content: Combined injectable contraceptives (CICs) are monthly injections that combine a progestin and an estrogen to prevent pregnancy. These contraceptives are designed to inhibit ovulation and alter the cervical mucus to reduce the likelihood of fertilization. Some of the brand names for these products include Cyclofem, Novafem, Mesigyna, and Lunelle. On October 5, 2000, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Lunelle™, a monthly contraceptive injection developed by Pharmacia. In April 2003, Pharmacia was acquired by Pfizer, the company that also manufactures Depo-Provera. However, by October 2003, Lunelle was discontinued in the United States. CICs are administered via intramuscular injection. The injection can be given in the deltoid muscle, the gluteus maximus, or the anterior thigh. For optimal effectiveness, the injection should ideally be administered every 28 to 30 days, although studies have shown that it remains effective for up to 33 days. The most common side effects associated with CICs are menstrual irregularities, particularly during the first three to six months of use. These irregularities may include changes in the frequency, duration, or intensity of menstrual bleeding. There are several formulations of combined injectable contraceptives, each containing different combinations of progestins and estrogens: Lunelle contains 25 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) and 5 mg of estradiol cypionate (E2C). Cyclofem contains 25 mg of depomedroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) and 5 mg of estradiol cypionate. Mesigyna contains 50 mg of norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN) and 5 mg of estradiol valerate. Deladroxate contains 150 mg of dihydroxyprogesterone acetophenide and 10 mg of estradiol enanthate.
